selectedCourses.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: Academic literacy,reflection,writing andpersonal/professionaldevelopment. Year1requirement,not specialistlegaltraining.

selectedCourses.name: Accounting & Corporate Finance
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces financial accounting, management accounting and investment appraisal, including accounting's social role and accountability implications. Students record transactions, prepare and interpret financial statements, and analyze performance and financing. The course then examines costing, pricing, budgeting, organizational control and sustainable management accounting. Investment decisions are evaluated using accounting and discounted-cash-flow measures. A case study analyzes the misuse of an accounting principle and its financial-statement effects.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: builds accounting and corporate-finance literacy explicitly identified in the Global Law and Business minor

selectedCourses.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. AI foundations and limitations lead into applications across enterprise functions and industries, labour-market change, productivity, innovation, market structure and inequality. Governance, corporate responsibility, regulation and future scenarios connect technological developments to institutional choices. Students analyze business cases and competing scholarly arguments, then investigate a country's AI readiness, workforce, regulation and industrial policy.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: AI business/economic change,labour markets,inequality,corporate responsibility andregulation provide a specific technology-governance context. The countryAI-readiness/regulation/industrial-policy project is not a specialist privacy/fairness or legal-technology course.

selectedCourses.name: Transnational Business Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies legal frameworks governing cross-border business transactions, combining comparative and international perspectives with practical legal problem-solving. Topics include trade regulation, contracts and international sales, transport and documentary transactions, finance, services, intellectual property, foreign investment and digital commerce. Advisory assignments assess contractual outcomes, risk allocation, intellectual-property protection and e-commerce compliance. A simulated arbitration develops written legal argument and oral advocacy.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: studies cross-border trade, contracts, investment, intellectual property, digital commerce and arbitration

selectedCourses.name: Money, Banking & Finance
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines financial markets and institutions, including the pricing of bonds, stocks and derivatives, interest rates and their risk and term structure, commercial-bank balance sheets and performance, financial structure and regulation, banking fragility and financial crises, central banks, money creation and monetary policy. Students apply algebraic and graphical analysis to financial and monetary problems. In the Stanford Banking Game they manage a simulated bank, analyse performance in Excel dashboards, forecast financial statements, and make evidence-based decisions about loans, deposits, capital, liquidity and risk. A small research project extends a selected financial or monetary research article through additional literature, a case study or updated evidence.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: develops finance and risk analysis for the commercial-law direction

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Economics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: establishes the economic context in which legal, business and sustainability rules operate

selectedCourses.name: Public Economics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: examines taxation, public goods, externalities and policy design relevant to public and environmental regulation

selectedCourses.name: Econometrics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: develops quantitative analysis for business, finance and regulatory evidence

selectedCourses.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: connects digital transformation and business strategy to technology-related legal and governance questions

selectedCourses.name: Market Research
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas. Ready to turn curiosity into career skills? Perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: provides applied research design and evidence analysis for commercial decision-making

selectedCourses.name: International Business & Governance
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines how international trade, globalization and political, sociocultural and technological forces shape firms' cross-border decisions. Economic foundations include trade theories, foreign direct investment, foreign exchange and the monetary system. Students analyze governance, responsibility and trade-policy conflicts, investigate an international-business question, and develop an evidence-based market-entry strategy covering country attractiveness and business functions. A tariff case applies game theory to stakeholder choices and negotiation.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: examines multinational firms, cross-border institutions and international business governance

selectedCourses.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions through the development of a startup concept. Students use design thinking to discover customer needs, define a problem, generate and prototype solutions, and construct value propositions and business models. Marketing, finance, operations, human resources and funding inform a coherent business plan and investor pitch. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: provides business foundations and the formal prerequisite for Transnational Business Law

selectedCourses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: establishes research design, statistics and evidence evaluation for the business and sustainability routes

selectedCourses.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines organizational behaviour at individual, group and organizational levels. Topics connect personality, perception, emotions and motivation to teams, leadership, power, conflict, structure, culture and change. Students design research plans for organizational cases and conduct a brief systematic literature review using PRISMA reporting tools. Workshops develop literature searching, study selection, source appraisal and synthesis, linking organizational-psychology evidence to practical questions and recommendations.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: studies organisational behaviour, leadership and responsibility inside firms

selectedCourses.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops negotiation as an analytical practice and interpersonal skill. Students learn interest-based bargaining, BATNA and ZOPA, value creation, framing, concessions and strategies for handling power, emotions and difficult counterparts. Social-psychological and communication perspectives connect negotiation to trust, ethics, culture and relationships. Frequent simulations and narrative analysis lead to an annotated negotiation film and the design, teaching and evaluation of a negotiation scenario grounded in Delta Climate Center themes.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: develops negotiation and strategic reasoning relevant to cross-border disputes and commercial practice

selectedCourses.name: Living with Water
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines how delta societies manage water risks and opportunities, using Zeeland as a central case. Physical and ecological challenges such as flooding, salinization, freshwater scarcity, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, considering trade-offs and long-term consequences. Site-based inquiry and a project apply these concepts to context-sensitive adaptation in a delta region.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: uses water governance and adaptation to examine how institutions respond to sustainability risks

selectedCourses.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: Collectivedecision-making,institutions,power,participation,justice andpublic/private responsibility are applied to food,water,energy andclimate cases. Consultation andpolicy advice develop governance analysis,not legalprocedure.

selectedCourses.name: Sustainability Essentials I
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: Planetaryboundaries,graphs/uncertainty,systems andphysical/chemical tools supply environmental evidence foundations. Biopolymerlaboratory work remains specific scientific study,notlegal analysis.

selectedCourses.name: Climate Change
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: Climateprocesses,impacts,mitigation/adaptation,climatejustice andgovernance provide direct factual/social problemknowledge for legal/environmental governance. Stakeholderinterview/film is not litigation training.

selectedCourses.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: Life-cycle assessment ofenvironmental,social,health andeconomic consequences supplies specific impact/evidence methods for circular-economy governance. Projects assess products/processes,notlegal compliance byassumption.

selectedCourses.name: Law, Society & Justice
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: surveys major fields of law and compares legal and social conceptions of justice

selectedCourses.name: Histories of Gender
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: North-American intersectional histories ofgender,slavery,family,sexuality,incarceration andactivism provide specific social/political contexts for rights andexclusion. This is not a globallegalhistory survey.

selectedCourses.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: studies human-rights treaties, institutions, case law and philosophical foundations

selectedCourses.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines the principles of criminal liability and the legal and moral bases of criminal justice. Students study criminal acts, causation and mental elements, legality, punishment, criminalization, justifications, excuses, inchoate offences and participation. A simulated legal-aid clinic applies doctrine to hypothetical facts through advice memoranda and oral argument. A criminology or organized-crime research proposal develops a literature review and methodology.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: studies criminal liability, legality, defences and criminal justice

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Public International Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces public international law through its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic legal systems. Legal principles are applied to responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection. The later course examines self-determination, Third World approaches, soft law, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises develop legal reasoning, while a research podcast critically investigates a political dimension of international law.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: studies public international law, sources, subjects, conflict, refugees and environmental law

selectedCourses.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: compares constitutional and administrative structures and rights across legal systems

selectedCourses.name: Principles of Private Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines property, tort and contract law through comparison of legal systems, primarily Germany, France, England, China and the United States. Students analyze rights and obligations, ownership, nuisance, negligence, contract formation and fairness, remedies and related policy pressures. Legal issue briefs apply the IRAC method. An issue-based comparative contract-law paper and simulated mediation develop comparative analysis, legal argument and negotiation.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: introduces private-law principles governing obligations, property, liability and transactions

selectedCourses.name: Foundations of European Union Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces the EU legal order through its institutions, sources, competences and relationship to member-state law. Students study supremacy, legal effect, liability and judicial remedies before applying citizenship and free-movement law to concrete problems. Structured legal cases and research into current judgments develop interpretation and comparison across EU and domestic settings. Digital regulation and the green transition provide a contemporary application.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: studies EU institutions, legal sources, market rules, rights and enforcement

selectedCourses.name: Ethics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: Historical/contemporary moraltheories,close reading andindependent ethicalargument supply normative evaluation ofresponsibility/justice. Environmental application is complementary; no dedicatedclimate-ethics syllabus is asserted.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: Originaltexts andnormative arguments about rights,authority,human nature andsociety provide specific philosophical/political foundations for evaluating law andglobaljustice. Not specialised jurisprudence.

selectedCourses.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: compares political institutions and state structures that underpin constitutional law

selectedCourses.name: Theory of International Relations
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: provides international-relations theory for analysing transnational institutions and conflict

selectedCourses.name: European Union Politics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: examines EU institutions, integration and political decision-making alongside EU law

selectedCourses.name: Public Policy Analysis
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: Description-only PublicPolicyAnalysis fullyconsidered: policyprocesses/alternativeconceptualisations through asugarcase andpolicymemos. A useful public-regulatory method/context,not anenvironmental-lawcourse.

selectedCourses.name: Peace & Conflict
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: studies international conflict, security, peace and institutional responses

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Sociology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: establishes social-scientific analysis of institutions, inequality and legal order

selectedCourses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: develops qualitative research design, interviewing and interpretation for socio-legal inquiry

selectedCourses.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: Social-movement theories,EnvironmentalJusticeAtlas cases,feminism,anti-colonialism anddegrowth supply specific collective-action/equity perspectives. No dedicated litigation practice is inferred.

selectedCourses.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: uses contemporary social theory to analyse institutions, power and legal-social change

selectedCourses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: develops structured oral argument, rhetorical analysis and audience-aware communication

selectedCourses.name: Persuasive Communication
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: develops advanced persuasive communication and evidence-based argument

selectedCourses.name: Media & the Environment
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines how visual, audiovisual, sound and digital media shape understanding of ecological problems and human-nonhuman relations. Environmental-humanities concepts guide close analysis of images, narratives and aesthetic strategies across cultural and historical contexts. Students investigate how scientific knowledge, risk and lived experience become representations that influence ethics, public debate and sustainability. A final analytical paper or media-based project develops an argument grounded in course theory.
selectedCourses.contributionFinding: analyses how environmental risks and sustainability claims are represented and debated

removedCoursesReviewed.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
removedCoursesReviewed.evidenceRead: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
removedCoursesReviewed.finding: Actualcontent considered before removal. Literary stylistics,geology/chemicalmaterials andunassignedsustainabilityresearch provide weakerimplementationofthis legal/governancequestion thanpoliticallegitimacy,climate,LCA,ethics andpolicy. No missingplanning-basedno-match.

removedCoursesReviewed.name: Dynamic Earth
removedCoursesReviewed.evidenceRead: Introduces Earth science by linking surface geology to deep-Earth and geophysical processes. Students study rocks, minerals, sedimentation, deformation, stratigraphy, plate tectonics, seismology, the mantle and core, and interactions with climate and other Earth systems. Field and practical work teaches observation and measurement, rock and mineral identification, and reconstruction of geological history. An Ardennes field investigation produces a geological cross-section, stratigraphic column and interpretive report.

removedCoursesReviewed.name: Earth's Resources
removedCoursesReviewed.evidenceRead: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.
removedCoursesReviewed.finding: Actualcontent considered before removal. Literary stylistics,geology/chemicalmaterials andunassignedsustainabilityresearch provide weakerimplementationofthis legal/governancequestion thanpoliticallegitimacy,climate,LCA,ethics andpolicy. removedCoursesReviewed.name: Sustainability Essentials II
removedCoursesReviewed.evidenceRead: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.

Literary stylistics,geology/chemicalmaterials andunassignedsustainabilityresearch provide weakerimplementationofthis legal/governancequestion thanpoliticallegitimacy,climate,LCA,ethics andpolicy. No missingplanning-basedno-match.

removedCoursesReviewed.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
removedCoursesReviewed.evidenceRead: Provides a research-project setting for sustainability questions supplied by organizations and companies in the Zeeland delta. Small teams work with an external advisor to review literature, formulate a research question, plan and execute an investigation, and develop a final product, design or report. The substantive topic and practical techniques depend on the partner project; the common focus is an evidence-based research process and engagement with external stakeholders.
removedCoursesReviewed.finding: Actualcontent considered before removal. Literary stylistics,geology/chemicalmaterials andunassignedsustainabilityresearch provide weakerimplementationofthis legal/governancequestion thanpoliticallegitimacy,climate,LCA,ethics andpolicy. No missingplanning-basedno-match.

removedCoursesReviewed.name: Style & Meaning
removedCoursesReviewed.evidenceRead: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.

UCR Ethics does not reproduce advanced philosophy of global law.
